ai_summary: Great Britain's total wind generation currently stands at 13.6 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 2.9 GW, accounting for 28.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust northern generation enables Scotland to deliver a pristine carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, sharply contrasting with the 54 gCO2/kWh observed GB-wide. However, cross-border transmission constraints continue to prevent this zero-carbon energy from reaching high-demand regions to the south. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 3,791 MWh through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring an immediate constraint cost of about £196,999. To replace this constrained volume, fossil-fueled generation had to be dispatched elsewhere across the network, consuming an estimated 720,309 m3 of gas and emitting an additional 1,327 tonnes CO2. Annualizing these figures points to a total yearly cost of curtailment of roughly £72 million. When socialized across nationwide electricity demand, this recurring transmission bottleneck increases UK invoices by an estimated £0.25/MWh, illustrating how grid infrastructure deficits impose ongoing financial costs on consumers while eroding the decarbonization benefits of renewable capacity.
